answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text: The proposed guidance does not clearly and definitively state whether consequential accounting is meant to convey additional information about the electricity purchases reported in the company’s Scope 2 GHG inventory or whether consequential accounting is meant to allow for offset-like claims for energy investments inside and outside of a company’s GHG inventory. If it is the latter, this guidance must have clear, prescriptive rules requiring companies to report which investments are included and excluded from their GHG inventories. Investments outside of a company’s inventory must also have more stringent additionality requirements to prevent double claims.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why secondary effects should be excluded
answers.text: Secondary effects should be allowed but not required to be quantified. Secondary effects are rarely modeled, can be challenging to model, and can involve a high degree of uncertainty. For example, changes in transmission and distribution emissions from changes in electricity procurement are simple to model and relatively concrete. In contrast, secondary impacts from renewable fuel procurement are difficult to model and depend on multiple variables that are unknown or uncertain. Therefore, requiring companies to model these effects increases reporting complexity while reducing reporting accuracy.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: Companies should be required to calculate and report these impacts annually. Annual reporting allows for adjustment to address grid transformation and the actual delivery of power. This also aligns with company goal-setting and reporting. Companies may choose to discuss potential impacts over the lifetime of the project separately.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text: The number and extent of additionality tests that should be required depends on whether this standard can be used to create offset-like claims. If the standard cannot be used to create these types of claims, the regulatory test and contractual/tenor test are sufficient to demonstrate additionality, as these prove that companies are not required to take these actions and that companies are investing in projects for a reasonable term. The financial test can be substituted for the regulatory test in cases where regulations are not fully enforced or can be met through other means, such as alternative compliance payments. Companies can use the common practice test to further illustrate how their investments decarbonize electric grids.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text: The positive list and performance standard tests will both require frequent updates to align with the current state of renewable energy. They also do not accommodate edge cases where a project does not meet all of the requirements of the list or standard but should be included in consequential accounting. answers.label: Claims possible under different test approaches
answers.text: Our preference is to not allow association claims but not overly restrict additionality for causal claims. Companies should have to take specific actions to use this standard, but the bar for what constitutes ‘action’ can be low. For example, signing up for a green utility product should allow a company to make a causal claim.

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text: Policy scenarios shift too often in political cycles. In addition, many policies have alternative mechanisms for compliance that don’t necessarily result in new electrical capacity. Both impact capacity modeling. Recent capacity additions are also easily accessible information.

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text: Project size and shape most closely match the characteristics of the project that relate to marginal emissions changes.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: The spatial granularity of the marginal emissions rate should match the spatial granularity of the consequential claim. We anticipate that consequential claims will not be more granular than the balancing authority level, as it will be difficult to obtain data and to model effects at higher granularity.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: The temporal granularity of the marginal emissions rate should match the temporal granularity of the consequential claim. The temporal granularity of the consequential claim depends on the type of grid intervention and the availability of temporal data. In markets with low renewable energy penetration, daily, monthly, or even annual temporal granularity may result in substantial changes to marginal emissions. In markets with high renewable energy penetration, companies will likely need to use hourly or sub-hourly granularity to demonstrate marginal emissions changes.

Why selected weighting approaches are infeasible
answers.text: Resource adequacy and intervention lifecycle approaches are difficult to model and are likely to contain too many assumptions to be reasonably comparable across company interventions.
